segs.e: Linked Discourses 11.1
Chapter One
With Suvīra
So I have heard.

segs.p: ekaṁ samayaṁ bhagavā sāvatthiyaṁ viharati jetavane anāthapiṇḍikassa ārāme.
segs.e: At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
There the Buddha addressed the mendicants,
“Mendicants!”
“Venerable sir,” they replied.
The Buddha said this:
“Once upon a time, mendicants, the titans marched against the gods.

segs.p: Atha kho, bhikkhave, sakko devānamindo suvīraṁ devaputtaṁ āmantesi:
segs.e: Then Sakka, lord of gods, addressed the godling Suvīra,
‘Dear Suvīra, the titans march against the gods!
Go, and march against the titans!’

segs.p: ‘Evaṁ, bhaddantavā’ti kho, bhikkhave, suvīro devaputto sakkassa devānamindassa paṭissutvā pamādaṁ āpādesi.
segs.e: ‘Yes, lord,’ replied Suvīra. But he fell into negligence.

segs.p: Dutiyampi kho, bhikkhave, sakko devānamindo suvīraṁ devaputtaṁ āmantesi:
segs.e: For a second time Sakka addressed Suvīra,
‘Dear Suvīra, the titans march against the gods!
Go, and march against the titans!’

segs.p: ‘Evaṁ, bhaddantavā’ti kho, bhikkhave, suvīro devaputto sakkassa devānamindassa paṭissutvā dutiyampi pamādaṁ āpādesi.
segs.e: ‘Yes, lord,’ replied Suvīra. But for a second time he fell into negligence.

segs.p: Tatiyampi kho, bhikkhave, sakko devānamindo suvīraṁ devaputtaṁ āmantesi:
segs.e: For a third time Sakka addressed Suvīra,
‘Dear Suvīra, the titans march against the gods!
Go, and march against the titans!’

segs.p: ‘Evaṁ, bhaddantavā’ti kho, bhikkhave, suvīro devaputto sakkassa devānamindassa paṭissutvā tatiyampi pamādaṁ āpādesi.
segs.e: ‘Yes, lord,’ replied Suvīra. But for a third time he fell into negligence.

segs.p: Atha kho, bhikkhave, sakko devānamindo suvīraṁ devaputtaṁ gāthāya ajjhabhāsi:
segs.e: Then Sakka addressed the godling Suvīra in verse:
‘Suvīra, go to that place
where you can achieve happiness
without working for it or trying hard—
and take me with you!’
‘That a lazy man who does no work,
and doesn’t do his duty,
can fulfill all his desires:
Sakka, render me this boon!’
‘Suvīra, go to that place
where a lazy man who does no work
prospers in unending happiness—
and take me with you!’
‘O Sakka, first among gods,
that we might find the happiness
that’s sorrowless, unstressed:
Sakka, render me this boon!’
‘If there exists anywhere a place
where one can live happily without working,
that surely would be extinguishment’s path!
Go there, Suvīra,
and take me with you!’

segs.p: So hi nāma, bhikkhave, sakko devānamindo sakaṁ puññaphalaṁ upajīvamāno devānaṁ tāvatiṁsānaṁ issariyādhipaccaṁ rajjaṁ kārento uṭṭhānavīriyassa vaṇṇavādī bhavissati.
segs.e: Since, mendicants, even that Sakka, lord of gods—while living off of the fruit of his good deeds, and ruling as sovereign lord over these gods of the thirty-three—will speak in praise of initiative and energy,

segs.p: Idha kho taṁ, bhikkhave, sobhetha, yaṁ tumhe evaṁ svākkhāte dhammavinaye pabbajitā samānā uṭṭhaheyyātha ghaṭeyyātha vāyameyyātha appattassa pattiyā anadhigatassa adhigamāya, asacchikatassa sacchikiriyāyā”ti.
segs.e: you can excel at this, for you who have gone forth in such a well explained teaching and training can try hard, strive, and make an effort to attain the unattained, achieve the unachieved, and realize the unrealized.”

Linked Discourses 11.3
Chapter One
The Banner’s Crest
At Sāvatthī.
There the Buddha addressed the mendicants,
“Mendicants!”
“Venerable sir,” they replied.
The Buddha said this:
“Once upon a time, mendicants, a battle was fought between the gods and the titans.

segs.p: Atha kho, bhikkhave, sakko devānamindo deve tāvatiṁse āmantesi:
segs.e: Then Sakka, lord of gods, addressed the gods of the thirty-three:

segs.p: ‘Sace, mārisā, devānaṁ saṅgāmagatānaṁ uppajjeyya bhayaṁ vā chambhitattaṁ vā lomahaṁso vā, mameva tasmiṁ samaye dhajaggaṁ ullokeyyātha.
segs.e: ‘Good fellows, when the gods are fighting, if you get scared or terrified, just look up at my banner’s crest.

segs.p: Mamañhi vo dhajaggaṁ ullokayataṁ yaṁ bhavissati bhayaṁ vā chambhitattaṁ vā lomahaṁso vā, so pahīyissati.
segs.e: Then your fear and terror will go away.

segs.p: No ce me dhajaggaṁ ullokeyyātha, atha pajāpatissa devarājassa dhajaggaṁ ullokeyyātha.
segs.e: If you can’t see my banner’s crest, then look up at the banner’s crest of the Progenitor, king of gods.

segs.p: Pajāpatissa hi vo devarājassa dhajaggaṁ ullokayataṁ yaṁ bhavissati bhayaṁ vā chambhitattaṁ vā lomahaṁso vā, so pahīyissati.
segs.e: Then your fear and terror will go away.

segs.p: No ce pajāpatissa devarājassa dhajaggaṁ ullokeyyātha, atha varuṇassa devarājassa dhajaggaṁ ullokeyyātha.
segs.e: If you can’t see his banner’s crest, then look up at the banner’s crest of Varuṇa, king of gods.

segs.p: Varuṇassa hi vo devarājassa dhajaggaṁ ullokayataṁ yaṁ bhavissati bhayaṁ vā chambhitattaṁ vā lomahaṁso vā, so pahīyissati.
segs.e: Then your fear and terror will go away.

segs.p: No ce varuṇassa devarājassa dhajaggaṁ ullokeyyātha, atha īsānassa devarājassa dhajaggaṁ ullokeyyātha.
segs.e: If you can’t see his banner’s crest, then look up at the banner’s crest of Īsāna, king of gods.

segs.p: Īsānassa hi vo devarājassa dhajaggaṁ ullokayataṁ yaṁ bhavissati bhayaṁ vā chambhitattaṁ vā lomahaṁso vā, so pahīyissatī’ti.
segs.e: Then your fear and terror will go away.’

segs.p: Taṁ kho pana, bhikkhave, sakkassa vā devānamindassa dhajaggaṁ ullokayataṁ, pajāpatissa vā devarājassa dhajaggaṁ ullokayataṁ, varuṇassa vā devarājassa dhajaggaṁ ullokayataṁ, īsānassa vā devarājassa dhajaggaṁ ullokayataṁ yaṁ bhavissati bhayaṁ vā chambhitattaṁ vā lomahaṁso vā, so pahīyethāpi nopi pahīyetha.
segs.e: However, when they look up at those banner’s crests their fear and terror might go away or it might not.
Why is that?

segs.p: Sakko hi, bhikkhave, devānamindo avītarāgo avītadoso avītamoho bhīru chambhī utrāsī palāyīti.
segs.e: Because Sakka is not free of greed, hate, and delusion. He is fearful, scared, nervous, quick to flee.
But, mendicants, I say this:

segs.p: ‘sace tumhākaṁ, bhikkhave, araññagatānaṁ vā rukkhamūlagatānaṁ vā suññāgāragatānaṁ vā uppajjeyya bhayaṁ vā chambhitattaṁ vā lomahaṁso vā, mameva tasmiṁ samaye anussareyyātha:
segs.e: If you’ve gone to a wilderness, or to the root of a tree, or to an empty hut and you get scared or terrified, just recollect me:

segs.p: “itipi so bhagavā arahaṁ sammāsambuddho vijjācaraṇasampanno sugato lokavidū anuttaro purisadammasārathi satthā devamanussānaṁ buddho bhagavā”ti.
segs.e: ‘That Blessed One is perfected, a fully awakened Buddha, accomplished in knowledge and conduct, holy, knower of the world, supreme guide for those fit for training, teacher of gods and humans, awakened, blessed.’

segs.p: Mamañhi vo, bhikkhave, anussarataṁ yaṁ bhavissati bhayaṁ vā chambhitattaṁ vā lomahaṁso vā, so pahīyissati.
segs.e: Then your fear and terror will go away.

segs.p: No ce maṁ anussareyyātha, atha dhammaṁ anussareyyātha:
segs.e: If you can’t recollect me, then recollect the teaching:

segs.p: “svākkhāto bhagavatā dhammo sandiṭṭhiko akāliko ehipassiko opaneyyiko paccattaṁ veditabbo viññūhī”ti.
segs.e: ‘The teaching is well explained by the Buddha—apparent in the present life, immediately effective, inviting inspection, relevant, so that sensible people can know it for themselves.’

segs.p: Dhammañhi vo, bhikkhave, anussarataṁ yaṁ bhavissati bhayaṁ vā chambhitattaṁ vā lomahaṁso vā, so pahīyissati.
segs.e: Then your fear and terror will go away.

segs.p: No ce dhammaṁ anussareyyātha, atha saṅghaṁ anussareyyātha:
segs.e: If you can’t recollect the teaching, then recollect the Saṅgha:

segs.p: “suppaṭipanno bhagavato sāvakasaṅgho ujuppaṭipanno bhagavato sāvakasaṅgho ñāyappaṭipanno bhagavato sāvakasaṅgho sāmīcippaṭipanno bhagavato sāvakasaṅgho, yadidaṁ cattāri purisayugāni aṭṭha purisapuggalā esa bhagavato sāvakasaṅgho, āhuneyyo pāhuneyyo dakkhiṇeyyo añjalikaraṇīyo anuttaraṁ puññakkhettaṁ lokassā”ti.
segs.e: ‘The Saṅgha of the Buddha’s disciples is practicing the way that’s good, direct, systematic, and proper. It consists of the four pairs, the eight individual persons. This is the Saṅgha of the Buddha’s disciples that is worthy of offerings dedicated to the gods, worthy of hospitality, worthy of a religious donation, worthy of greeting with cupped palms, and is the supreme field of merit for the world.’

segs.p: Saṅghañhi vo, bhikkhave, anussarataṁ yaṁ bhavissati bhayaṁ vā chambhitattaṁ vā lomahaṁso vā, so pahīyissati.
segs.e: Then your fear and terror will go away.
Why is that?

segs.p: Tathāgato hi, bhikkhave, arahaṁ sammāsambuddho vītarāgo vītadoso vītamoho abhīru acchambhī anutrāsī apalāyī’”ti.
segs.e: Because the Realized One is free of greed, hate, and delusion. He is fearless, brave, bold, and stands his ground.”
That is what the Buddha said.

segs.p: Idaṁ vatvāna sugato athāparaṁ etadavoca satthā:
segs.e: Then the Holy One, the Teacher, went on to say:
“In the wilderness, at a tree’s root,
or an empty hut, O mendicants,
recollect the Buddha,
and no fear will come to you.
If you can’t recollect the Buddha—
the eldest in the world, the captain of men—
then recollect the teaching,
emancipating, well taught.
If you can’t recollect the teaching—
emancipating, well taught—
then recollect the Saṅgha,
the supreme field of merit.
Thus recollecting the Buddha,
the teaching, and the Saṅgha, mendicants,
fear and terror
and goosebumps will be no more.”
Linked Discourses 11.4
Chapter One
With Vepacitti
At Sāvatthī.
“Once upon a time, mendicants, a battle was fought between the gods and the titans.

segs.p: Atha kho, bhikkhave, vepacitti asurindo asure āmantesi:
segs.e: Then Vepacitti, lord of titans, addressed the titans,

segs.p: ‘sace, mārisā, devānaṁ asurasaṅgāme samupabyūḷhe asurā jineyyuṁ devā parājineyyuṁ, yena naṁ sakkaṁ devānamindaṁ kaṇṭhapañcamehi bandhanehi bandhitvā mama santike āneyyātha asurapuran’ti.
segs.e: ‘My good fellows, if the titans defeat the gods in this battle, bind Sakka, the lord of gods, by his limbs and neck and bring him to my presence in the citadel of the titans.’

segs.p: Sakkopi kho, bhikkhave, devānamindo deve tāvatiṁse āmantesi:
segs.e: Meanwhile, Sakka, lord of gods, addressed the gods of the thirty-three,

segs.p: ‘sace, mārisā, devānaṁ asurasaṅgāme samupabyūḷhe devā jineyyuṁ asurā parājineyyuṁ, yena naṁ vepacittiṁ asurindaṁ kaṇṭhapañcamehi bandhanehi bandhitvā mama santike āneyyātha sudhammasabhan’ti.
segs.e: ‘My good fellows, if the gods defeat the titans in this battle, bind Vepacitti by his limbs and neck and bring him to my presence in the Hall of Clear Right of the gods.’

segs.p: Tasmiṁ kho pana, bhikkhave, saṅgāme devā jiniṁsu, asurā parājiniṁsu.
segs.e: In that battle the gods won and the titans lost.

segs.p: Atha kho, bhikkhave, devā tāvatiṁsā vepacittiṁ asurindaṁ kaṇṭhapañcamehi bandhanehi bandhitvā sakkassa devānamindassa santike ānesuṁ sudhammasabhaṁ.
segs.e: So the gods of the thirty-three bound Vepacitti by his limbs and neck and brought him to Sakka’s presence in the Hall of Clear Right of the gods.

segs.p: Tatra sudaṁ, bhikkhave, vepacitti asurindo kaṇṭhapañcamehi bandhanehi baddho sakkaṁ devānamindaṁ sudhammasabhaṁ pavisantañca nikkhamantañca asabbhāhi pharusāhi vācāhi akkosati paribhāsati.
segs.e: And as Sakka was entering and leaving the hall, Vepacitti abused and insulted him with rude, harsh words.

segs.p: Atha kho, bhikkhave, mātali saṅgāhako sakkaṁ devānamindaṁ gāthāhi ajjhabhāsi:
segs.e: So Mātali the chariot handler addressed Sakka in verse:
‘O Maghavā, O Sakka,
is it from fear or from weakness
that you endure such harsh words
in the presence of Vepacitti?’
‘It’s not out of fear or weakness
that I’m patient with Vepacitti.
For how can a sensible person like me
get in a fight with a fool?’
‘Fools would vent even more
if there’s no one to put a stop to them.
So an attentive one should stop
a fool with forceful punishment.’
‘I think that this is the only way
to put a stop to a fool,
when you know that the other is upset,
be mindful and stay calm.’
‘In this mere endurance, Vāsava,
I see a flaw.
When a fool thinks,
“He endures me out of fear,”
the simpleton will go after you even harder,
like a cow chasing someone who runs away.’
‘Let him think this if he wishes, or not—
“He endures me out of fear.”
For the highest goal, one’s own,
naught better than patience is found.
When a strong person
endures a weakling,
they call that the ultimate patience,
for a weakling must always be patient.
The strength of folly
is really just weakness, they say.
But no one can challenge a person
who’s strong, guarded by the teaching.
When you get angry at an angry person
you just make things worse for yourself.
When you don’t get angry at an angry person
you win a battle hard to win.
When you know that the other is angry,
you act for the good of both
yourself and the other
if you’re mindful and stay calm.
People inexpert in the teaching
consider one who heals both
oneself and the other
to be a fool.’

segs.p: So hi nāma, bhikkhave, sakko devānamindo sakaṁ puññaphalaṁ upajīvamāno devānaṁ tāvatiṁsānaṁ issariyādhipaccaṁ rajjaṁ kārento khantisoraccassa vaṇṇavādī bhavissati.
segs.e: Since, mendicants, even that Sakka, lord of gods—while living off of the fruit of his good deeds, and ruling as sovereign lord over these gods of the thirty-three—will speak in praise of patience and gentleness,

segs.p: Idha kho taṁ, bhikkhave, sobhetha yaṁ tumhe evaṁ svākkhāte dhammavinaye pabbajitā samānā khamā ca bhaveyyātha soratā cā”ti.
segs.e: you can excel at this, for you who have gone forth in such a well explained teaching and training can develop patience and gentleness.”

Chapter One
Victory by Good Speech
At Sāvatthī.
“Once upon a time, mendicants, a battle was fought between the gods and the titans.

segs.p: Atha kho, bhikkhave, vepacitti asurindo sakkaṁ devānamindaṁ etadavoca:
segs.e: Then Vepacitti, lord of titans, said to Sakka, lord of gods,
‘Lord of gods, let there be victory by fine words!’
‘Vepacitti, let there be victory by fine words!’

segs.p: Atha kho, bhikkhave, devā ca asurā ca pārisajje ṭhapesuṁ:
segs.e: Then the gods and the titans appointed a panel of judges, saying,
‘These will understand our good and bad statements.’

segs.p: Atha kho, bhikkhave, vepacitti asurindo sakkaṁ devānamindaṁ etadavoca:
segs.e: Then Vepacitti, lord of titans, said to Sakka, lord of gods,
‘Lord of gods, recite a verse!’

segs.p: Evaṁ vutte, bhikkhave, sakko devānamindo vepacittiṁ asurindaṁ etadavoca:
segs.e: When he said this, Sakka said to him,
‘Vepacitti, you are the elder gods here.
Recite a verse.’

segs.p: Evaṁ vutte, bhikkhave, vepacitti asurindo imaṁ gāthaṁ abhāsi:
segs.e: So Vepacitti spoke this verse:
‘Fools would vent even more
if there’s no one to put a stop to them.
So an intelligent person should stop
a fool with forceful punishment.’

segs.e: The titans applauded Vepacitti’s verse, while the gods kept silent.

segs.p: Atha kho, bhikkhave, devānañca asurānañca pārisajjā etadavocuṁ:
segs.e: Then the panel of judges consisting of both gods and titans said this,
‘The verses spoken by Vepacitti

segs.p: Tā ca kho sadaṇḍāvacarā sasatthāvacarā, iti bhaṇḍanaṁ iti viggaho iti kalaho.

Bird Nests
At Sāvatthī.
“Once upon a time, mendicants, a battle was fought between the gods and the titans.

segs.p: Tasmiṁ kho pana, bhikkhave, saṅgāme asurā jiniṁsu, devā parājiniṁsu.
segs.e: In that battle the titans won and the gods lost.

segs.p: Parājitā ca kho, bhikkhave, devā apāyaṁsveva uttarenamukhā, abhiyaṁsveva ne asurā.
segs.e: Defeated, the gods fled north with the titans in pursuit.

segs.p: Atha kho, bhikkhave, sakko devānamindo mātali saṅgāhakaṁ gāthāya ajjhabhāsi:
segs.e: Then Sakka, lord of gods, addressed his chariot handler Mātali in verse:
‘Mātali, don’t ram the bird nests
in the Red Silk-Cotton Woods with your draft-pole.
I’d rather give up our lives to the titans
than deprive these birds of their nests.’

segs.p: ‘Evaṁ, bhaddantavā’ti kho, bhikkhave, mātali saṅgāhako sakkassa devānamindassa paṭissutvā sahassayuttaṁ ājaññarathaṁ paccudāvattesi.
segs.e: ‘Yes, lord,’ replied Mātali. And he turned the chariot back around, with its team of a thousand thoroughbreds.
Then the titans thought,

segs.p: ‘paccudāvatto kho dāni sakkassa devānamindassa sahassayutto ājaññaratho.
segs.e: ‘Now Sakka’s chariot has turned back.

segs.p: Dutiyampi kho devā asurehi saṅgāmessantī’ti bhītā asurapurameva pāvisiṁsu.
segs.e: The titans will have to fight the gods a second time!’ Terrified, they retreated right away to the citadel of the titans.

segs.p: Iti kho, bhikkhave, sakkassa devānamindassa dhammena jayo ahosī”ti.
segs.e: And that’s how Sakka came to win victory by principle.”

segs.p: “Bhūtapubbaṁ, bhikkhave, sakkassa devānamindassa rahogatassa paṭisallīnassa evaṁ cetaso parivitakko udapādi:

segs.p: ‘yopi me assa supaccatthiko tassapāhaṁ na dubbheyyan’ti.
segs.e: ‘I should never betray even a sworn enemy.’

segs.p: Atha kho, bhikkhave, vepacitti asurindo sakkassa devānamindassa cetasā cetoparivitakkamaññāya yena sakko devānamindo tenupasaṅkami.

segs.e: Sakka saw Vepacitti coming off in the distance,
and said to him,
‘Stop, Vepacitti, you’re caught!’

segs.p: ‘Yadeva te, mārisa, pubbe cittaṁ, tadeva tvaṁ mā pajahāsī’ti.

segs.p: “Bhūtapubbaṁ, bhikkhave, sambahulā isayo sīlavanto kalyāṇadhammā araññāyatane paṇṇakuṭīsu sammanti.
segs.e: “Once upon a time, mendicants, several seers who were ethical, of good character, settled in leaf huts in a wilderness region.

segs.p: Atha kho, bhikkhave, sakko ca devānamindo vepacitti ca asurindo yena te isayo sīlavanto kalyāṇadhammā tenupasaṅkamiṁsu.
segs.e: Then Sakka, lord of gods, and Vepacitti, lord of titans, went to those seers.

segs.p: Atha kho, bhikkhave, vepacitti asurindo paṭaliyo upāhanā ārohitvā khaggaṁ olaggetvā chattena dhāriyamānena aggadvārena assamaṁ pavisitvā te isayo sīlavante kalyāṇadhamme apabyāmato karitvā atikkami.
segs.e: Vepacitti put on his lined sandals, strapped on his sword, and, carrying a sunshade, entered the hermitage through the main gate. He walked right past those seers, keeping them at arm’s length.

segs.p: Atha kho, bhikkhave, sakko devānamindo paṭaliyo upāhanā orohitvā khaggaṁ aññesaṁ datvā chattaṁ apanāmetvā dvāreneva assamaṁ pavisitvā te isayo sīlavante kalyāṇadhamme anuvātaṁ pañjaliko namassamāno aṭṭhāsi.
segs.e: Sakka took off his lined sandals, gave his sword to others, and, putting down his sunshade, entered the hermitage through the same gate. He stood downwind of those seers, revering them with cupped palms.

segs.p: Atha kho, bhikkhave, te isayo sīlavanto kalyāṇadhammā sakkaṁ devānamindaṁ gāthāya ajjhabhāsiṁsu:
segs.e: Then those seers addressed Sakka in verse:
‘When seers have been long initiated,
the odor of their bodies goes with the gale.
You’d better leave, O thousand-eyed!
The odor of the seers is unclean, king of gods.’
‘When seers have been long initiated,
let the odor of their bodies go with the gale.
We yearn for this odor, sirs,
like a colorful crown of flowers.
The gods don’t see it as repulsive.’”

Chapter One

At Sāvatthī.

segs.p: “Bhūtapubbaṁ, bhikkhave, sambahulā isayo sīlavanto kalyāṇadhammā samuddatīre paṇṇakuṭīsu sammanti.
segs.e: “Once upon a time, mendicants, several seers who were ethical, of good character, settled in leaf huts on the ocean shore.

segs.p: Tena kho pana samayena devāsurasaṅgāmo samupabyūḷho ahosi.
segs.e: Now at that time a battle was fought between the gods and the titans.

segs.p: Atha kho, bhikkhave, tesaṁ isīnaṁ sīlavantānaṁ kalyāṇadhammānaṁ etadahosi:
segs.e: Then the seers thought,
‘The gods are principled, the titans are unprincipled.
We may be at risk from the titans.

segs.p: Yannūna mayaṁ sambaraṁ asurindaṁ upasaṅkamitvā abhayadakkhiṇaṁ yāceyyāmā’ti.
segs.e: Why don’t we approach Sambara, lord of titans, and beg him for a pledge of safety?’

segs.p: Atha kho, bhikkhave, te isayo sīlavanto kalyāṇadhammā—seyyathāpi nāma balavā puriso samiñjitaṁ vā bāhaṁ pasāreyya, pasāritaṁ vā bāhaṁ samiñjeyya; evameva—samuddatīre paṇṇakuṭīsu antarahitā sambarassa asurindassa sammukhe pāturahesuṁ.
segs.e: Then, as easily as a strong person would extend or contract their arm, those seers vanished from those leaf huts on the ocean shore and reappeared in Sambara’s presence.

segs.p: Atha kho, bhikkhave, te isayo sīlavanto kalyāṇadhammā sambaraṁ asurindaṁ gāthāya ajjhabhāsiṁsu:
segs.e: Then those seers addressed Sambara in verse:
‘The seers have come to Sambara
to beg for a pledge of safety.
For you can give them what you wish,
whether danger or safety.’
‘There is no safety for seers,
the hated associates of Sakka!
Though you beg me for your safety,
I’ll only give you fear!’
‘Though we beg you for our safety,
you give us only fear.
This is what we get from you:
may endless peril come to you!
Whatever kind of seed you sow,
that is the fruit you reap.
A doer of good gets good,
a doer of bad gets bad.
You, my dear, have sown your own seed,
now you’ll experience the fruit.’

segs.p: Atha kho, bhikkhave, te isayo sīlavanto kalyāṇadhammā sambaraṁ asurindaṁ abhisapitvā—seyyathāpi nāma balavā puriso samiñjitaṁ vā bāhaṁ pasāreyya, pasāritaṁ vā bāhaṁ samiñjeyya; evameva—sambarassa asurindassa sammukhe antarahitā samuddatīre paṇṇakuṭīsu pāturahesuṁ.
segs.e: Then those seers, having cursed Sambara, as easily as a strong person would extend or contract their arm, vanished from Sambara’s presence and reappeared in those leaf huts on the ocean shore.

segs.p: Atha kho, bhikkhave, sambaro asurindo tehi isīhi sīlavantehi kalyāṇadhammehi abhisapito rattiyā sudaṁ tikkhattuṁ ubbijjī”ti.
segs.e: But after being cursed by the seers, Sambara woke in alarm three times that night.”

segs.p: “Sakkassa, bhikkhave, devānamindassa pubbe manussabhūtassa satta vatapadāni samattāni samādinnāni ahesuṁ, yesaṁ samādinnattā sakko sakkattaṁ ajjhagā.
segs.e: “Mendicants, in a former life, when Sakka was a human being, he undertook seven vows. And it was because of undertaking these that he achieved the status of Sakka.
What seven?
As long as I live, may I support my parents.
As long as I live, may I honor the elders in the family.
As long as I live, may I speak gently.
As long as I live, may I not backbite.

segs.p: yāvajīvaṁ vigatamalamaccherena cetasā agāraṁ ajjhāvaseyyaṁ muttacāgo payatapāṇi vossaggarato yācayogo dānasaṁvibhāgarato,
segs.e: As long as I live, may I live at home with heart rid of the stain of stinginess, freely generous, open-handed, loving to let go, committed to charity, loving to give and to share.
As long as I live, may I speak the truth.

segs.p: yāvajīvaṁ akkodhano assaṁ—sacepi me kodho uppajjeyya, khippameva naṁ paṭivineyyanti.
segs.e: As long as I live, may I be free of anger, or should anger arise, may I quickly get rid of it.

segs.p: Sakkassa, bhikkhave, devānamindassa pubbe manussabhūtassa imāni satta vatapadāni samattāni samādinnāni ahesuṁ, yesaṁ samādinnattā sakko sakkattaṁ ajjhagāti.

and has given up backbiting;
who’s committed to getting rid of stinginess,
is truthful, and has mastered anger:
the gods of the thirty-three declare
them to be a true person.”

Poor

segs.p: Ekaṁ samayaṁ bhagavā rājagahe viharati veḷuvane kalandakanivāpe.
segs.e: At one time the Buddha was staying near Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the squirrels’ feeding ground.
There the Buddha addressed the mendicants,
“Mendicants!”
“Venerable sir,” they replied.
The Buddha said this:

segs.p: “Bhūtapubbaṁ, bhikkhave, aññataro puriso imasmiṁyeva rājagahe manussadaliddo ahosi manussakapaṇo manussavarāko.
segs.e: “Once upon a time, mendicants, there was a poor person, destitute and pitiful.

segs.p: So tathāgatappavedite dhammavinaye saddhaṁ samādiyi, sīlaṁ samādiyi, sutaṁ samādiyi, cāgaṁ samādiyi, paññaṁ samādiyi.
segs.e: They took up faith, ethics, learning, generosity, and wisdom in the teaching and training proclaimed by the Realized One.

segs.p: So tathāgatappavedite dhammavinaye saddhaṁ samādiyitvā sīlaṁ samādiyitvā sutaṁ samādiyitvā cāgaṁ samādiyitvā paññaṁ samādiyitvā kāyassa bhedā paraṁ maraṇā sugatiṁ saggaṁ lokaṁ upapajji devānaṁ tāvatiṁsānaṁ sahabyataṁ.
segs.e: After undertaking these things, when their body broke up, after death, they were reborn in a good place, a heavenly realm, in the company of the gods of the thirty-three.

segs.p: So aññe deve atirocati vaṇṇena ceva yasasā ca.
segs.e: There they outshone the other gods in beauty and glory.

segs.p: Tatra sudaṁ, bhikkhave, devā tāvatiṁsā ujjhāyanti khiyyanti vipācenti:
segs.e: But the gods of the thirty-three complained, grumbled, and objected,
‘Oh lord, how incredible, how amazing!

segs.p: Ayañhi devaputto pubbe manussabhūto samāno manussadaliddo ahosi manussakapaṇo manussavarāko;
segs.e: For when this godling was a human being in their past life they were poor, destitute, and pitiful.

segs.p: so kāyassa bhedā paraṁ maraṇā sugatiṁ saggaṁ lokaṁ upapanno devānaṁ tāvatiṁsānaṁ sahabyataṁ.
segs.e: And when their body broke up, after death, they were reborn in a good place, a heavenly realm, in the company of the gods of the thirty-three.

segs.p: So aññe deve atirocati vaṇṇena ceva yasasā cā’ti.
segs.e: Here they outshine the other gods in beauty and glory.’

segs.p: Atha kho, bhikkhave, sakko devānamindo deve tāvatiṁse āmantesi:
segs.e: Then Sakka, lord of gods, addressed the gods of the thirty-three,

segs.p: ‘mā kho tumhe, mārisā, etassa devaputtassa ujjhāyittha.
segs.e: ‘Good fellows, don’t complain about this godling.

segs.p: Eso kho, mārisā, devaputto pubbe manussabhūto samāno tathāgatappavedite dhammavinaye saddhaṁ samādiyi, sīlaṁ samādiyi, sutaṁ samādiyi, cāgaṁ samādiyi, paññaṁ samādiyi.
segs.e: When this godling was a human being in their past life they took up faith, ethics, learning, generosity, and wisdom in the teaching and training proclaimed by the Realized One.

segs.p: So tathāgatappavedite dhammavinaye saddhaṁ samādiyitvā sīlaṁ samādiyitvā sutaṁ samādiyitvā cāgaṁ samādiyitvā paññaṁ samādiyitvā kāyassa bhedā paraṁ maraṇā sugatiṁ saggaṁ lokaṁ upapanno devānaṁ tāvatiṁsānaṁ sahabyataṁ.
segs.e: After undertaking these things, when their body broke up, after death, they’ve been reborn in a good place, a heavenly realm, in the company of the gods of the thirty-three.

segs.p: So aññe deve atirocati vaṇṇena ceva yasasā cā’ti.
segs.e: Here they outshine the other gods in beauty and glory.’

segs.p: Atha kho, bhikkhave, sakko devānamindo deve tāvatiṁse anunayamāno tāyaṁ velāyaṁ imā gāthāyo abhāsi:
segs.e: Then Sakka, lord of gods, guiding the gods of the thirty-three, spoke this verse:
‘Whoever has faith in the Realized One,
unwavering and well grounded;
whose ethical conduct is good,
praised and loved by the noble ones;
who has confidence in the Saṅgha,
and correct view:
they’re said to be prosperous,
their life is not in vain.
So let the wise devote themselves
to faith, ethical behaviour,
confidence, and insight into the teaching,
remembering the instructions of the Buddhas.’”

Chapter Two
Delightful
Near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove.

segs.p: Atha kho sakko devānamindo yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā bhagavantaṁ abhivādetvā ekamantaṁ aṭṭhāsi. Ekamantaṁ ṭhito kho sakko devānamindo bhagavantaṁ etadavoca:
segs.e: And then Sakka, lord of gods, went up to the Buddha, bowed, stood to one side, and said to him,
“Sir, what is a delightful place?”
“Shrines in parks and forests,
well-made lotus ponds,
are not worth a sixteenth part
of a delightful human being.
Whether in village or wilderness,
in a valley or the uplands,
wherever the perfected ones live
is a delightful place.”

Chapter Two
Sponsoring Sacrifice

segs.p: Ekaṁ samayaṁ bhagavā rājagahe viharati gijjhakūṭe pabbate.
segs.e: At one time the Buddha was staying near Rājagaha, on the Vulture’s Peak Mountain.

segs.p: Atha kho sakko devānamindo yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā bhagavantaṁ abhivādetvā ekamantaṁ aṭṭhāsi.
segs.e: And then Sakka, lord of gods, went up to the Buddha, bowed, stood to one side,

segs.p: Ekamantaṁ ṭhito kho sakko devānamindo bhagavantaṁ gāthāya ajjhabhāsi:
segs.e: and addressed him in verse:
“For humans, those merit-seeking creatures,
who sponsor sacrifices,
making worldly merit,
where is a gift very fruitful?”
“Four practicing the path,
and four established in the fruit.
This is the upright Saṅgha,
with wisdom, ethics, and immersion.
For humans, those merit-seeking creatures,
who sponsor sacrifices,
making worldly merit,
what is given to the Saṅgha is very fruitful.”
Linked Discourses 11.17
Chapter Two
Homage to the Buddha
Near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove.

segs.p: Tena kho pana samayena bhagavā divāvihāragato hoti paṭisallīno.
segs.e: Now at that time the Buddha had gone into retreat for the day’s meditation.

segs.p: Atha kho sakko ca devānamindo brahmā ca sahampati yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkamiṁsu; upasaṅkamitvā paccekaṁ dvārabāhaṁ nissāya aṭṭhaṁsu.
segs.e: Then Sakka, lord of gods, and the divinity Sahampati approached the Buddha and stationed themselves one by each door-post.

segs.p: Atha kho sakko devānamindo bhagavato santike imaṁ gāthaṁ abhāsi:
segs.e: Then Sakka spoke this verse in the Buddha’s presence:
“Rise, hero! Victor in battle, with burden put down,
wander the world free of debt.
Your mind is fully liberated,
like the moon on the fifteenth night.”
“Lord of gods, that’s not how to pay homage to the Realized Ones.
This is how it should be done:
‘Rise, hero! Victor in battle, caravan leader,
wander the world free of debt.
Let the Blessed One teach the Dhamma!
There will be those who understand!’”
Linked Discourses 11.18
Chapter Two
Homage of Householders
At Sāvatthī.

segs.p: “bhūtapubbaṁ, bhikkhave, sakko devānamindo mātaliṁ saṅgāhakaṁ āmantesi:
segs.e: “Once upon a time, mendicants, Sakka, lord of gods, addressed his chariot handler Mātali,

segs.p: ‘yojehi, samma mātali, sahassayuttaṁ ājaññarathaṁ. Uyyānabhūmiṁ gacchāma subhūmiṁ dassanāyā’ti.
segs.e: ‘My dear Mātali, harness the chariot with its team of a thousand thoroughbreds. We will go to a park and see the scenery.’

segs.p: ‘Evaṁ, bhaddantavā’ti kho, bhikkhave, mātali saṅgāhako sakkassa devānamindassa paṭissutvā sahassayuttaṁ ājaññarathaṁ yojetvā sakkassa devānamindassa paṭivedesi:
segs.e: ‘Yes, lord,’ replied Mātali. He harnessed the chariot and informed Sakka,
‘Good fellow, the chariot with its team of a thousand thoroughbreds has been harnessed.
Please go at your convenience.’

segs.p: Atha kho, bhikkhave, sakko devānamindo vejayantapāsādā orohanto añjaliṁ katvā sudaṁ puthuddisā namassati.
segs.e: Then Sakka descended from the Palace of Victory, raised his cupped palms, and revered the various quarters.

segs.p: Atha kho, bhikkhave, mātali saṅgāhako sakkaṁ devānamindaṁ gāthāya ajjhabhāsi:
segs.e: So Mātali the chariot handler addressed Sakka in verse:
‘Those proficient in the three Vedas worship you,
as do all the aristocrats on earth,
the four great kings,
and the glorious host of Thirty.
So what’s the name of the spirit
that you worship, Sakka?’
‘Those proficient in the three Vedas worship me,
as do all the aristocrats on earth,
the four great kings,
and the glorious host of Thirty.
But I revere those accomplished in ethics,
who have long trained in immersion,
who have rightly gone forth
for the culmination of spiritual life.
I also worship those householders,
the ethical lay followers
who make merit, Mātali,
providing for a partner in a principled manner.’
‘Those who you worship
seem to be the best in the world, Sakka.
I too will worship
those who you worship, Sakka.’
After saying this, Maghavā the chief,
king of gods, Sujā’s husband,
having worshiped the various quarters
climbed into his chariot.”

Chapter Two
Homage of the Teacher
Near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove.

segs.p: “Bhūtapubbaṁ, bhikkhave, sakko devānamindo mātaliṁ saṅgāhakaṁ āmantesi:
segs.e: “Once upon a time, mendicants, Sakka, lord of gods, addressed his chariot handler Mātali,

segs.p: ‘yojehi, samma mātali, sahassayuttaṁ ājaññarathaṁ, uyyānabhūmiṁ gacchāma subhūmiṁ dassanāyā’ti.
segs.e: ‘My dear Mātali, harness the chariot with its team of a thousand thoroughbreds. We will go to a park and see the scenery.’

segs.p: ‘Evaṁ, bhaddantavā’ti kho, bhikkhave, mātali saṅgāhako sakkassa devānamindassa paṭissutvā sahassayuttaṁ ājaññarathaṁ yojetvā sakkassa devānamindassa paṭivedesi:
segs.e: ‘Yes, lord,’ replied Mātali. He harnessed the chariot and informed Sakka,
‘Good fellow, the chariot with its team of a thousand thoroughbreds has been harnessed.
Please go at your convenience.’

segs.p: Atha kho, bhikkhave, sakko devānamindo vejayantapāsādā orohanto añjaliṁ katvā sudaṁ bhagavantaṁ namassati.
segs.e: Then Sakka descended from the Palace of Victory, raised his cupped palms, and revered the Buddha.

segs.p: Atha kho, bhikkhave, mātali saṅgāhako sakkaṁ devānamindaṁ gāthāya ajjhabhāsi:
segs.e: So Mātali the chariot handler addressed Sakka in verse:
‘Gods and men
worship you, Vāsava.
So what’s the name of the spirit
that you worship, Sakka?’
‘It’s the fully awakened Buddha,
the Teacher of peerless name
in this world with its gods—
that’s who I worship, Mātali.
Those in whom greed, hate, and ignorance
have faded away;
the perfected ones with defilements ended—
they’re who I worship, Mātali.
The trainees who enjoy reducing suffering,
diligently pursuing the training
for getting rid of greed and hate,
and going past ignorance—
they’re who I worship, Mātali.’
‘Those who you worship
seem to be the best in the world, Sakka.
I too will worship
those who you worship, Sakka.’
After saying this, Maghavā the chief,
king of gods, Sujā’s husband,
having worshiped the Buddha,
climbed into his chariot.”

Chapter Two
Homage of the Saṅgha
Near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove.

segs.p: “bhūtapubbaṁ, bhikkhave, sakko devānamindo mātaliṁ saṅgāhakaṁ āmantesi:
segs.e: “Once upon a time, mendicants, Sakka, lord of gods, addressed his chariot handler Mātali,

segs.p: ‘yojehi, samma mātali, sahassayuttaṁ ājaññarathaṁ, uyyānabhūmiṁ gacchāma subhūmiṁ dassanāyā’ti.
segs.e: ‘My dear Mātali, harness the chariot with its team of a thousand thoroughbreds. We will go to a park and see the scenery.’

segs.p: ‘Evaṁ, bhaddantavā’ti kho, bhikkhave, mātali saṅgāhako sakkassa devānamindassa paṭissutvā, sahassayuttaṁ ājaññarathaṁ yojetvā sakkassa devānamindassa paṭivedesi:
segs.e: ‘Yes, lord,’ replied Mātali. He harnessed the chariot and informed Sakka,
‘Good fellow, the chariot with its team of a thousand thoroughbreds has been harnessed.
Please go at your convenience.’

segs.p: Atha kho, bhikkhave, sakko devānamindo vejayantapāsādā orohanto añjaliṁ katvā sudaṁ bhikkhusaṅghaṁ namassati.
segs.e: Then Sakka descended from the Palace of Victory, raised his cupped palms, and revered the mendicant Saṅgha.

segs.p: Atha kho, bhikkhave, mātali saṅgāhako sakkaṁ devānamindaṁ gāthāya ajjhabhāsi:
segs.e: So Mātali the chariot handler addressed Sakka in verse:
‘It’s these who should worship you,
namely the humans stuck in their putrid bodies,
sunk in a carcass,
stricken by hunger and thirst.
Why then do you envy those
who are homeless, Vāsava?
Relate the seers’ way of life,
let us hear what you say.’
‘This is why I envy the
homeless, Mātali.
When they leave a village,
they proceed without concern.
They hoard no goods in storerooms,
nor in pots or baskets.
They seek food prepared by others,
and, true to their vows, live on that.
The attentive, whose words are full of wisdom,
live peacefully and quietly.
Gods fight with titans,
and mortals fight each other, Mātali.
Not fighting among those who fight,
quenched among those who have taken up arms,
not grasping among those who grasp:
they’re who I worship, Mātali.’
‘Those who you worship
seem to be the best in the world, Sakka.
I too will worship
those who you worship, Vāsava.’
After saying this, Maghavā the chief,
king of gods, Sujā’s husband,
having worshiped the mendicant Saṅgha,
climbed into his chariot.”
Linked Discourses 11.21
Chapter Three
Slain
Near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove.

segs.p: Atha kho sakko devānamindo yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā bhagavantaṁ abhivādetvā ekamantaṁ aṭṭhāsi.
segs.e: And then Sakka, lord of gods, went up to the Buddha, bowed, stood to one side,

segs.p: Ekamantaṁ ṭhito kho sakko devānamindo bhagavantaṁ gāthāya ajjhabhāsi:
segs.e: and addressed him in verse:
“When what is slain do you sleep at ease?
When what is slain is there no sorrow?
What is the one thing
whose killing you approve?”
“When anger’s slain you sleep at ease.
When anger’s slain there is no sorrow.
Anger has a poisonous root
and a sweet tip, O Vāsava.
The noble ones praise its killing,
for when it’s slain there is no sorrow.”
Linked Discourses 11.22
Chapter Three
Ugly
Near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove.

segs.p: “bhūtapubbaṁ, bhikkhave, aññataro yakkho dubbaṇṇo okoṭimako sakkassa devānamindassa āsane nisinno ahosi.
segs.e: “Once upon a time, mendicants, there was a native spirit who was ugly and deformed. He sat on the throne of Sakka, lord of gods.

segs.p: Tatra sudaṁ, bhikkhave, devā tāvatiṁsā ujjhāyanti khiyyanti vipācenti:
segs.e: But the gods of the thirty-three complained, grumbled, and objected,
‘Oh lord, how incredible, how amazing!

segs.p: Ayaṁ yakkho dubbaṇṇo okoṭimako sakkassa devānamindassa āsane nisinno’ti.
segs.e: This ugly and deformed spirit is sitting on the throne of Sakka, the lord of gods.’

segs.p: Yathā yathā kho, bhikkhave, devā tāvatiṁsā ujjhāyanti khiyyanti vipācenti tathā tathā so yakkho abhirūpataro ceva hoti dassanīyataro ca pāsādikataro ca.
segs.e: But the more the gods complained, the more attractive, good-looking, and lovely that spirit became.

segs.p: Atha kho, bhikkhave, devā tāvatiṁsā yena sakko devānamindo tenupasaṅkamiṁsu; upasaṅkamitvā sakkaṁ devānamindaṁ etadavocuṁ:
segs.e: So the gods went up to Sakka and told him what had happened. He replied,

segs.p: ‘idha te, mārisa, aññataro yakkho dubbaṇṇo okoṭimako sakkassa devānamindassa āsane nisinno.
Tatra sudaṁ, mārisa, devā tāvatiṁsā ujjhāyanti khiyyanti vipācenti:
Ayaṁ yakkho dubbaṇṇo okoṭimako sakkassa devānamindassa āsane nisinno”ti.
Yathā yathā kho, mārisa, devā ujjhāyanti khiyyanti vipācenti tathā tathā so yakkho abhirūpataro ceva hoti dassanīyataro ca pāsādikataro cāti.
So hi nūna, mārisa, kodhabhakkho yakkho bhavissatī’ti.
segs.e: ‘Surely, good fellow, that must be the anger-eating spirit!’

segs.p: Atha kho, bhikkhave, sakko devānamindo yena so kodhabhakkho yakkho tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā ekaṁsaṁ uttarāsaṅgaṁ karitvā dakkhiṇajāṇumaṇḍalaṁ pathaviyaṁ nihantvā yena so kodhabhakkho yakkho tenañjaliṁ paṇāmetvā tikkhattuṁ nāmaṁ sāveti:
segs.e: Then Sakka went up to that spirit, arranged his robe over one shoulder, knelt on his right knee, raised his joined palms toward the anger-eating spirit, and pronounced his name three times:
‘Good fellow, I am Sakka, lord of gods! Good fellow, I am Sakka, the lord of gods!’

segs.p: Yathā yathā kho, bhikkhave, sakko devānamindo nāmaṁ sāvesi tathā tathā so yakkho dubbaṇṇataro ceva ahosi okoṭimakataro ca.
segs.e: But the more Sakka pronounced his name, the uglier and more deformed the spirit became,

segs.p: Dubbaṇṇataro ceva hutvā okoṭimakataro ca tatthevantaradhāyīti.
segs.e: until eventually it vanished right there.

segs.p: Atha kho, bhikkhave, sakko devānamindo sake āsane nisīditvā deve tāvatiṁse anunayamāno tāyaṁ velāyaṁ imā gāthāyo abhāsi:
segs.e: Then Sakka, lord of gods, guiding the gods of the thirty-three, spoke this verse:
‘My mind isn’t easily upset;
I’m not easily drawn into the maelstrom.
I don’t get angry for long,
anger doesn’t last in me.
When I do get angry I don’t speak harshly,
nor do I advertise my own virtues.
I carefully restrain myself
out of regard for my own welfare.’”
Linked Discourses 11.23
Chapter Three
The Sambari Sorcery
At Sāvatthī.
The Buddha said this:

segs.p: “bhūtapubbaṁ, bhikkhave, vepacitti asurindo ābādhiko ahosi dukkhito bāḷhagilāno.
segs.e: “Once upon a time, mendicants, Vepacitti, lord of titans, was sick, suffering, gravely ill.

segs.p: Atha kho, bhikkhave, sakko devānamindo yena vepacitti asurindo tenupasaṅkami gilānapucchako.
segs.e: So Sakka went to see him to ask after his illness.

segs.p: Addasā kho, bhikkhave, vepacitti asurindo sakkaṁ devānamindaṁ dūratova āgacchantaṁ.
segs.e: Vepacitti saw Sakka coming off in the distance,
and said to him,
‘Heal me, lord of gods!’
‘Teach me, Vepacitti, the Sambari sorcery.’

segs.p: ‘Na tāvāhaṁ vācemi, yāvāhaṁ, mārisa, asure paṭipucchāmī’ti.
segs.e: ‘I can’t do that, good fellow, until I have consulted with the titans.’

segs.p: Atha kho, bhikkhave, vepacitti asurindo asure paṭipucchi:
segs.e: Then Vepacitti, lord of titans, asked the titans,
‘Good fellows, may I teach the Sambari sorcery to Sakka, lord of gods?’

segs.p: ‘Mā kho tvaṁ, mārisa, vācesi sakkaṁ devānamindaṁ sambarimāyan’ti.
segs.e: ‘Do not, good fellow, teach the Sambari sorcery to Sakka!’

segs.p: Atha kho, bhikkhave, vepacitti asurindo sakkaṁ devānamindaṁ gāthāya ajjhabhāsi:
segs.e: So Vepacitti addressed Sakka in verse:
‘O Maghavā, O Sakka,
king of gods, Sujā’s husband:
a sorceror like Sambara falls
into the terrible hell for a full century.’”
Linked Discourses 11.24
Chapter Three
Transgression
At Sāvatthī.

segs.p: Tena kho pana samayena dve bhikkhū sampayojesuṁ.
segs.e: Now at that time two mendicants had clashed.
One of them transgressed against the other.

segs.p: Atha kho so bhikkhu tassa bhikkhuno santike accayaṁ accayato deseti;
segs.e: The transgressor confessed to the other mendicant,
but they didn’t accept it.

segs.p: Atha kho sambahulā bhikkhū yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkamiṁsu; upasaṅkamitvā bhagavantaṁ abhivādetvā ekamantaṁ nisīdiṁsu. Ekamantaṁ nisinnā kho te bhikkhū bhagavantaṁ etadavocuṁ:
segs.e: Then several mendicants went up to the Buddha, bowed, sat down to one side, and told him what had happened.

segs.p: “idha, bhante, dve bhikkhū sampayojesuṁ, tatreko bhikkhu accasarā.
Atha kho so, bhante, bhikkhu tassa bhikkhuno santike accayaṁ accayato deseti, so bhikkhu nappaṭiggaṇhātī”ti.

segs.e: “Mendicants, there are two fools.

segs.p: Yo ca accayaṁ accayato na passati, yo ca accayaṁ desentassa yathādhammaṁ nappaṭiggaṇhāti—
segs.e: One who doesn’t recognize when they’ve made a mistake. And one who doesn’t properly accept the confession of someone who’s made a mistake.
These are the two fools.
There are two who are astute.

segs.p: Yo ca accayaṁ accayato passati, yo ca accayaṁ desentassa yathādhammaṁ paṭiggaṇhāti—
segs.e: One who recognizes when they’ve made a mistake. And one who properly accepts the confession of someone who’s made a mistake.
These are the two who are astute.

segs.p: Bhūtapubbaṁ, bhikkhave, sakko devānamindo sudhammāyaṁ sabhāyaṁ deve tāvatiṁse anunayamāno tāyaṁ velāyaṁ imaṁ gāthaṁ abhāsi:
segs.e: Once upon a time, mendicants, Sakka, lord of gods, guiding the gods of the thirty-three, spoke this verse:
‘Control your anger;
don’t let friendships decay.
Don’t blame the blameless,
and don’t backbite.
For anger crushes bad people
like a mountain.’”
Linked Discourses 11.25
Chapter Three
Don’t Be Angry
So I have heard.

segs.p: ekaṁ samayaṁ bhagavā sāvatthiyaṁ viharati jetavane anāthapiṇḍikassa ārāme.
segs.e: At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.

segs.p: Tatra kho bhagavā bhikkhū …pe… bhagavā etadavoca:
segs.e: There the Buddha addressed the mendicants:

segs.p: “bhūtapubbaṁ, bhikkhave, sakko devānamindo sudhammāyaṁ sabhāyaṁ deve tāvatiṁse anunayamāno tāyaṁ velāyaṁ imaṁ gāthaṁ abhāsi:
segs.e: “Once upon a time, mendicants, Sakka, lord of gods, guiding the gods of the thirty-three, spoke this verse:
‘Don’t let anger be your master,
don’t get angry at angry people.
Kindness and harmlessness
are always present in the noble ones.
For anger crushes bad people
like a mountain.’”
